extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural historians, stone-sculptors, and students of architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, technical principles, and aesthetic criteria for designing and carving cornices and capitals (especially Venetian/Byzantine/Gothic types), covering profile, ornament placement, execution methods, proportion, and expressive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy of execution / faithful energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The chiselling should show energy and a 'faithful energy' — keen, true, every line sharp and right; not an accumulation of feeble action or dulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast energetic chiselling (e.g., cornices a and d: 'The man who cut those two uppermost cornices ... His work is absolutely unreprovable; keen, and true, as Nature's own') with the indolent copyist (e.g., the inlay worker at b who will 'stay where he is for ever'). Energetic work may be achieved even in limited time but must avoid bluntness or error in curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism versus conventionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament should be natural and suggestive of real forms rather than being mere conventionalised patterns (e.g., Greek egg-and-arrow is 'a nonsense cornice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer designs that suggest true images (clusters of leaves with central depression visible) rather than arbitrary repeats of forms that have no relation to the thing they purport to represent. Naturalism may require fewer incisions but clearer intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestiveness and economy of incision
rubrics_metrics.description: With the fewest possible incisions, the ornament should suggest the true image (e.g., clusters of leaves each with its central depression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive incisions that merely decorate without suggesting form; well-directed chiselling that retains necessary lines beneath turned-over leaves produces clear ribs on the upper surface while preserving under-surface incisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility at distance and in varied light
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptural details should be 'distinctly visible at almost any distance from the eye, and in almost any light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and cut leaves and ribs so that their essential forms register clearly from typical viewing distances and lighting conditions; small delicate finishes that vanish at distance are less effective for architectural ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding mere copyism
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that is merely copied from classical patterns without original temper or spirit leads to stagnation and lifelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically reproduce Greek or Roman motifs (e.g., eggs and arrows) without reinterpreting them; copyism yields 'lifeless mechanism' while original energetic work moves style forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent intention in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament must have a 'consistent intention'—every incision and form should serve a coherent expressive purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with less overall work, consistent intention yields meaningful ornament; scattershot decoration without unity undermines the design's communicative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile vs ornament relationship (overlay/under-profile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration may be represented as overlaid on an early profile (having its own outside contour) or incised from the outside profile—i.e., the ornament may have an under-profile and a separate leaf-profile laid over it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When leaf-decoration overlays an older profile, the simpler under-profile should often remain visible or suggested; designers should conceive both contours (under-profile and leaf-profile) so the parts join coherently (e.g., 'made up of two ogee curves laid, head to tail').

rubrics_metrics.name: Two technical methods to conceal cornice-wall junction
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome meagreness at the junction of cornice and wall, either use a projecting roll at the foot of the cornice or slip the whole cornice slightly forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two methods lead to two groups of cornices/capitals and should be chosen according to desired profile and subsequent ornamentation. Implementing a roll or forward slip produces a 'bar of shadow' that visually strengthens the junction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth/proportion adjustments when converting cornice to capital
rubrics_metrics.description: A cornice becoming a capital must have depth added to its profile to reach the just proportion of the shaft head; small Greek egg cornices are 'utterly incapable' of becoming capitals without total change of form and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting cornice profiles into capitals, designers must adjust depth appropriately; misapplications (as in Renaissance pilaster heads) produce mean or disfigured heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaf contour indicates derivation (cornice vs capital)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the leaf contour matches certain profiles (examples 10–12 vs 7–9), the cornice may be derived from a capital or vice versa; capitals may be concentrations of cornices, and cornices may be unrolled capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study leaf contour to determine whether a profile is 'actually of a capital, or of a cornice derived from a capital' versus 'actually of a cornice or of a capital derived from a cornice.' This affects how profiles and ornament relate historically and functionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two families of capitals determined by ornament position
rubrics_metrics.description: Two real orders: those with ornament left outside the bell (concave/Doric family) and those with ornament cut into the bell (convex/Corinthian family); these are distinguished also by concave or convex bell contours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether ornament will form the external contour (convex) or be projected from the concave bell; this choice has structural and stylistic consequences and defines the family's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of ornamentation (vesica piscis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornamental portions should fall between the dotted lines and the pointed oval (vesica piscis) traced by them—this is the 'Limit of ornamentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep ornament contained within these theoretical limits so the profile and its strength are preserved; do not let ornament overflow the established geometrical bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of ornament relative to profile (Doric vs concave)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a profile whose contour is composed of the ornamentation (Doric/convex), the ornament must be rich and close enough to form a continuous surface; on a concave bell, ornament must be sparing and dispersed to allow the bell to be seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-ornamenting a concave bell (which chokes the profile) and avoid under-ornamenting a convex/profile-forming surface (which weakens its massy character). Wrong density will 'approximate it to its opposite.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Style consequences of cutting order (execution method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of execution influences style: the concave-school sculptor prepares masses and conceives ornament beforehand (leading to symmetry and accuracy); the convex-school sculptor works incisions like pencil touches on a smooth bell (leading to freedom but possible irregularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For concave profiles, finish the smooth bell first then return to projecting pieces; for convex, incise freely but be wary of irregular, rude handling. Execution order is a practical determinant of the ornament's final character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural implications of deep incisions or projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep incisions into an already hollowed profile weaken its supporting power; leaving projecting bits outside a bulging profile may destroy its relation to the original sloping line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose ornament position and depth so as not to compromise strength or ruin the essential profile; structural considerations constrain acceptable ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chamfering harsh projecting angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh projecting angles (e.g., an added abacus) should be softened with the simplest chamfer on the visible side only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying a chamfer resolves projecting harshness while preserving the intended profile; used historically to refine added abaci and avoid ugly sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of curls and leaf-turning to express upper ribs
rubrics_metrics.description: When leaves curl over, retain old incisions below to represent the under-surface; when they turn over, carve true ribs on the top of the leaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique produces believable leaf anatomy and demonstrates 'quick steps' toward naturalism (e.g., 'Look at the upper and under surface of a cabbage-leaf').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of truncations/spurs with leafing
rubrics_metrics.description: Truncations and spurs may be treated by reducing them to vegetable outlines and laying four healing leaves upon the wounds, evolving into one of the loveliest Gothic capital groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using leaves on truncations harmonises sharp truncations with the overall vegetative motif; the spurred types have varied plans and often incorporate vegetal or animal forms for richer effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-specific vs generic leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves in southern work may be non-specific or change species within one composition (e.g., cabbage to ivy), a 'clearly classical element' distinct from northern preference for oak/ivy/apple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to depict a particular botanical species (northern realism) or a generalized classical leaf (southern/classical tradition). Consider whether mixed-species leaves serve a legitimate figurative purpose in architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office/position determines ornament scale, not necessarily age
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation from bold cornice projection to modest capital service often reflects office and position rather than chronological age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing profiles, consider function (cornice vs capital) to explain differences in leaf projection and outline, rather than assuming temporal precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of disciplined symmetry and imaginative licence
rubrics_metrics.description: The concave/disciplinarian school enforces symmetry and precision but risks formalism; the convex/liberal school allows imagination and variety but risks irregularity and licentiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to balance the strengths of both approaches: disciplined order where needed, and freedom where it enables richer expressive development. Beware degeneracy into 'lifeless mechanism' or 'licentiousness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional planning for order and execution quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of working methods (especially in concave profiles), sculptors should 'conceive beforehand all that he has to do' thereby achieving a definite symmetrical order and skilful execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior planning of the whole ornament leads to better arrangement and accuracy; on concave projects, sequence work so delicate projecting parts are finished after the smoother bell is prepared to avoid breakage.
